claims.text: Equiatomic FeNiCrMn has a single-phase FCC initial structure over 77–300 K.
The initial FeNiCrMn crystal contains a background population of vacancy clusters.
The HCP-like regions in deformed FeNiCrMn are intrinsic stacking faults rather than FCC-to-HCP martensite.
Intrinsic stacking faults in FeNiCrMn are stabilized by negative or near-zero stacking-fault energy at low temperatures.
The maximum yield stress is governed by the critical stress for Shockley-partial nucleation at pre-existing vacancy clusters.
Shockley partials nucleate at vacancy clusters because their local stress concentration lowers the nucleation barrier.
Decreasing temperature lowers the stacking-fault energy and promotes stacking faults and partial-dislocation-mediated deformation.
Low stacking-fault energy makes intrinsic stacking faults energetically preferable to full-dislocation glide or phase transformation.
The <11-1> loading orientation produces a higher maximum yield stress than the <110> orientation.
The <11-1> orientation has a larger resolved shear-stress component on the {111}<112> slip system than the <110> orientation.
A larger resolved shear-stress component for <11-1> causes a higher macroscopic stress to be required to reach the critical partial-nucleation threshold.
The HCP-like regions are transient stacking faults that do not complete the lattice rearrangement required for martensitic transformation.
Post-yield deformation will produce a high density of intrinsic stacking faults.
Post-yield regions will lack long-range HCP periodicity, distinct HCP diffraction peaks, and continuous HCP lattice-parameter shifts.
Yield strength is relatively insensitive to strain rate between 10^8 and 10^10 s^-1.
Yield strength decreases monotonically as temperature increases from cryogenic to ambient conditions.
Kinetic barriers can keep an FCC alloy metastable even when the HCP phase is thermodynamically favored.
A continuous, long-range HCP lattice would discriminate true martensitic transformation from isolated stacking faults bounded by partial dislocations.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described both as containing a background density of vacancy clusters and as a perfect FCC lattice. A lattice containing vacancy clusters is not defect-free; the intended controlled-defect state needs clarification.

The intervention and prediction invoke comparison across 10^8–10^10 s^-1, but the conditions and falsification design specify only 10^8 s^-1, so the proposed experiment cannot test the strain-rate-insensitivity claim.

The stated orientation rationale is internally mechanically inconsistent: for a fixed critical resolved shear stress, a larger resolved-shear factor normally implies a lower required macroscopic stress, whereas the hypothesis uses it to predict a higher macroscopic yield stress.
